planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; wild daffodil is native to deciduous woodlands and damp meadows across Western Europe, from England and France to Spain and Portugal, where it blooms so early in the season that it earned the common name Lent Lily. It naturalizes readily in grass and light woodland shade, increasing into drifts over the years if left undisturbed through its summer dormancy.

directions: Plant bulbs in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; wild daffodil is the ancestral species standing behind nearly all modern large-trumpet (Division 1) daffodil cultivars, bearing a single drooping flower per stem in which the slightly twisted, pale-yellow perianth segments are distinctly shorter and paler than the deeper golden-yellow trumpet corona, giving the bicolor effect typical of the species. Native to woodland margins, hedgerows, and unimproved meadows from the British Isles through France to Iberia, it has long naturalized in old orchards, churchyards, and pastures, flowering in late winter to early spring ahead of most garden daffodils. Allow the foliage to die back fully and leave established colonies undisturbed in grass or light woodland shade, where it slowly spreads by both bulb offsets and seed into increasingly dense drifts.

subcategory: autumn-blooming nocturnal North African daffodil species

planting.note: Plant bulbs in late summer to early fall in gritty, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; green flowered narcissus is native to coastal cliffs and dry scrub of Morocco and the Rock of Gibraltar and flowers in autumn rather than spring, so bulbs should be kept completely dry and dormant through summer before being watered back into growth as nights cool. Best grown in a bulb frame or container where its need for a bone-dry summer rest can be guaranteed.

directions: Plant in gritty, fast-draining, lean soil in full sun and withhold water completely through the summer dormancy; green flowered narcissus is one of the most unusual species in the genus, producing narrow, rush-like, nearly leafless stems topped by small, star-shaped, yellow-green flowers with a greatly reduced corona reduced almost to a ring at the base of the perianth segments. Unlike nearly all other daffodils it blooms in autumn, its strongly sweet fragrance intensifying after dark to attract night-flying moths, its principal pollinators. Native to dry, rocky coastal habitats in Morocco and on the Rock of Gibraltar, it is rare in general cultivation and grown mainly by specialist bulb collectors in pots or bulb frames where its need for summer-dry, winter-wet conditions can be met precisely.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in late summer to early fall in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; autumn narcissus is native to dry, rocky, and sandy sites throughout the Mediterranean Basin and flowers in autumn, typically appearing leafless or just ahead of its grass-like foliage. Give it a completely dry summer rest and protect from prolonged winter wet, as it is adapted to a hot, dry-summer Mediterranean climate.

directions: Plant small bulbs in gritty, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun with a dry summer dormancy; autumn narcissus produces slender, leafless or near-leafless stems in early to mid autumn, each bearing one or two small, white, star-like flowers with widely spread perianth segments and a small, flat, yellow-to-orange cup at the center. Native to dry rocky slopes, garrigue, and sandy coastal ground across the Mediterranean Basin from Iberia and southern France to Italy, Greece, and North Africa, it is one of the earliest of the autumn-flowering bulb species to bloom each year, often appearing before the first autumn rains have properly softened the ground. Best suited to a sunny, well-drained rock garden, raised bed, or bulb frame where summer baking and sharp winter drainage can both be guaranteed.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in gritty, sharply drained, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; rush-leaved jonquil is native to sunny, rocky limestone slopes and garrigue in Spain and southern France and is intolerant of wet, heavy soils, especially during its summer dormancy. Excellent for raised beds, rock gardens, and alpine troughs where drainage can be kept sharp.

directions: Plant small bulbs in gritty, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; rush-leaved jonquil is a diminutive species named for its narrow, cylindrical, rush-like leaves, which distinguish it from the flatter-leaved jonquilla. Each short stem carries one to three small, strongly fragrant, bright-yellow flowers with a flattish cup, opening in early to mid spring on sunny rocky slopes across its native range in Spain and southern France. Native to thin, dry, often limestone soils in full sun, it requires excellent drainage and a baked-dry summer rest to thrive, making it best suited to rock gardens, raised beds, or alpine troughs rather than ordinary border conditions. Left undisturbed, it slowly forms tight, floriferous clumps that return reliably each spring.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; least daffodil is native to mountain meadows and rocky slopes of the Pyrenees and northern Spain, where it is among the earliest daffodils to flower each year. It is well suited to rock gardens, alpine troughs, and the front of borders, and naturalizes readily in short grass.

directions: Plant small bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; least daffodil is a true miniature trumpet species, standing only a few inches tall and bearing a single small flower per stem in which the slightly twisted, pale-yellow perianth segments are shorter than the deeper golden trumpet corona, echoing the proportions of the larger wild daffodil in diminutive scale. Native to mountain pastures and rocky, grassy slopes of the Pyrenees and northern Spain, it flowers very early in spring, often among the first daffodils to open. It is a reliable, long-lived choice for rock gardens, alpine troughs, and the edges of borders, and will naturalize slowly in fine, undisturbed turf.
